topics.title: Pythagoras: problem solving
topics.intro: Pythagoras’ theorem is easy once the triangle is drawn: the hard part of a problem is spotting the right-angled triangle hidden in a ladder, a field, a walk or a box, and deciding whether to add or subtract. Always sketch it, label the hypotenuse, then calculate.
topics.teach: Explain how you decide whether to add or subtract the squares, using a ladder against a wall as your example.
topics.talk: Find right angles at home: a door, a bookcase, a screen. Ask her to estimate a diagonal, then work it out from the width and height.
topics.hook: **Sketch, label, decide**: find the right angle, mark the hypotenuse (opposite it, the longest side), then **finding the longest side? add; finding a shorter side? subtract**.

visual.caption: A ladder against a wall: the ladder is the hypotenuse. Height² = ladder² − ground².

topics.title: Reverse percentages
topics.intro: In a reverse percentage problem you know the amount AFTER a percentage change and need the amount BEFORE. The trap is taking the percentage of the new amount. Instead, the new amount is a known percentage of the original (80% after 20% off, 120% after a 20% rise), so divide by the multiplier.
topics.teach: Explain why £80 after 20% off was not £96 before, and how to find the real original price.
topics.talk: In a shop or online, look at a sale price and ask her what the price was before the discount.
topics.hook: **After → before: DIVIDE by the multiplier.** 20% off means × 0.8, so undo it with ÷ 0.8. Never take the percentage of the new price.

visual.caption: £48 is 4 of the 5 boxes (80%), so one box is £12 and the original is 5 × £12 = £60. In one step: £48 ÷ 0.8 = £60.

topics.title: Drawing linear graphs and parallel lines
topics.intro: To draw a straight-line graph, make a table of values (choose three x-values, work out y), plot the points and join them with a ruler. Parallel lines have the same gradient. Lines like x = 3 are vertical and y = 3 horizontal.
topics.teach: Explain how you would draw y = 2x − 1 from scratch, and how to tell which other lines are parallel to it.
topics.talk: Ask her to draw y = x + 1 and y = x − 2 on squared paper and say what she notices.
topics.hook: **Same m, parallel.** A table of three points: if they are not in a straight line, one is wrong. **x = number is vertical; y = number is horizontal.**

visual.caption: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3: both have gradient 2, so they are parallel. Only the y-intercept is different.

topics.title: Gradient and y-intercept
topics.intro: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (how steep: how far up for each 1 across) and c is the y-intercept (where it crosses the y-axis). Get y on its own first. From two points, gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.
topics.teach: Explain what the 3 and the −2 mean in y = 3x − 2, and how to find the gradient between two points.
topics.talk: A phone contract costs £10 a month plus £5 to start. Ask her to write it as y = mx + c and say what m and c mean.
topics.hook: **m = mountain** (how steep), **c = crossing** (where it crosses the y-axis). Gradient = **up ÷ across** (rise over run).

visual.caption: y = ½x − 1: it crosses the y-axis at −1, and goes up 1 for every 2 across, so the gradient is ½.

topics.title: Estimation
topics.intro: Estimate by rounding every number to 1 significant figure, then calculate in your head. Estimates check calculator answers: if they are wildly different, something went wrong. Dividing by a number less than 1 makes the answer bigger.
topics.teach: Explain how to estimate 38.7 ÷ 0.48, and why the answer is bigger than 38.7.
topics.talk: At the supermarket, ask her to estimate the total of three items before you reach the till.
topics.hook: **1 s.f. first, then calculate.** Dividing by 0.5 is the same as doubling.

topics.title: Lines of symmetry
topics.intro: A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves match exactly. Rotational symmetry counts how many times a shape fits onto itself in one full turn. A regular polygon has as many lines of symmetry as sides. Reflections use a mirror line: each point ends up the same distance away on the other side.
topics.teach: Explain why a rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry and not 4, and why a parallelogram has none.
topics.talk: Fold paper shapes together: a rectangle along its diagonal, a square, a kite. Which folds match?
topics.hook: **Fold test**: if the halves do not match exactly, it is not a line of symmetry. A rectangle’s diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry. **Regular n-gon: n lines, order n.**

visual.caption: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry (3 through opposite corners, 3 through the middles of opposite sides) and rotational symmetry of order 6.

topics.title: Solving equations
topics.intro: Solve an equation by doing the same to both sides until x is alone: undo + and − first, then × and ÷. With brackets, expand first; with x on both sides, move the smaller x term; with fractions, multiply through. Always check by substituting your answer back.
topics.teach: Explain how to solve 5(x − 2) = 3(x + 4), step by step, and how to check your answer.
topics.talk: Play “think of a number”: she sets you a puzzle (“I double it and add 7 and get 31”), and you write and solve the equation.
topics.hook: **Balance**: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. **Check by substituting**: both sides must come out equal.

topics.title: Using a calculator
topics.intro: A scientific calculator follows the order of operations, so you must add brackets round the top and bottom of a fraction. Then read the display carefully: money needs two decimal places, 0.5 hours is 30 minutes, E means × 10 to a power, and real answers sometimes need rounding up (you cannot hire 7.2 coaches).
topics.teach: Explain how to type (23.4 + 8.9) ÷ (5.2 − 1.7) into a calculator, and why −3² gives −9.
topics.talk: Ask her to work out the cost per item of a multipack on a calculator, and to round it sensibly.
topics.hook: **Bracket the top, bracket the bottom.** Then: does the answer make sense? Estimate to check.

topics.title: Angles in triangles
topics.intro: The angles in any triangle add up to 180°. In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal; in an equilateral triangle every angle is 60°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles opposite it.
topics.teach: Explain why an exterior angle of a triangle equals the two opposite interior angles added together.
topics.talk: Ask her to tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them together on a straight line.
topics.hook: **Triangle 180, straight line 180, round a point 360.** Isosceles: **two equal sides, two equal angles**.

topics.title: Fraction calculations
topics.intro: Add and subtract fractions with a common denominator. Multiply tops and bottoms. To divide, flip the second fraction and multiply. Turn mixed numbers into improper fractions first, and simplify at the end.
topics.teach: Explain how to work out 2⅓ ÷ ¾, and why dividing by a fraction can make a number bigger.
topics.talk: Halve or scale up a recipe together, using the fractions in it.
topics.hook: **Add/subtract: same bottom. Multiply: straight across. Divide: Keep, Change, Flip.**
